name: arping
desc: Utility to check whether MAC addresses are already taken on a LAN
why: A door into ARP: asking the LAN who has an address and seeing duplicate MACs answer back.

brief.what_it_is: Arping is a command-line ARP utility, written in C, that checks whether an IPv4 address on the local network segment is in use and reports which MAC address answers for it. It sends ARP who-has requests to the LAN and prints the is-at replies it gets back. The README also describes a second mode that goes the other way: pinging a raw MAC address with a broadcast ICMP echo, sent in an Ethernet frame addressed only to that MAC, to learn which IP it uses. The Homebrew description says it checks whether MAC addresses are taken, but the README's main framing is IP-to-MAC probing.
brief.why_it_exists: Thomas Habets wrote it because plain ping fails when a host blocks ICMP, or when you are on a non-routable net, and ARP cache entries are a more reliable signal. He also gives a catch-22 use case: someone with a block of real IANA addresses cannot ping an address before taking it, and cannot pick a free one without knowing which are taken.
brief.how_it_works: For an IP target, arping broadcasts an ARP 'who-has' request and waits for an 'is-at' reply, which the README shows with tcpdump captures. For a MAC target, it sends an ICMP echo request to a broadcast IP (255.255.255.255 or an address given with -T) inside an Ethernet frame addressed to the target MAC, and the target's echo reply reveals its IP. The README notes that many OSes do not answer broadcast pings the expected way, so -T may need tuning, and it suggests a brute-force loop over -T addresses.

brief.install_notes: Requires libnet 1.1 or newer and libpcap; the README points to github.com/libnet/libnet and tcpdump.org, or the distro packages. Build uses ./configure, and the README refers to an INSTALL file for details. Sending raw packets normally needs root. The author suggests either running it as root or granting CAP_NET_RAW on Linux (libnet 1.1.5+), and he advises against making it setuid. For MAC pings on Linux, /proc/sys/net/ipv4/icmp_echo_ignore_broadcasts must be 0 on the target. The Windows .exe linked from the FAQ was not built by the author.
brief.standout: It explains ARP-level probing clearly with real tcpdump traces and a candid FAQ. The MAC-ping trick, which sends an ICMP broadcast inside a unicast frame to a chosen MAC, reveals an IP for a host that may ignore ICMP otherwise. The author is open about its limits, down to the libnet quirks and timing accuracy.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release date and I did not check the releases or commit history. It mentions a 2.09 tarball, tests on IRIX and OpenBSD sparc64 dated 2009, and a mailing list. The Homebrew formula name and description are present, but I have no recent-activity evidence either way.
brief.caveats: Round-trip times are imprecise, sometimes off by milliseconds, because the program only sees packets once the kernel hands them over. Pinging a raw MAC depends on the target answering broadcast ICMP, which many systems do not do. Arping 1.x (libnet 1.0) is gone from the current tarball; you need 2.08 for it. It does not answer for localhost or your own MAC. The author tests on Debian, Ubuntu on ARM, and OpenBSD, and says other platforms should work but are not regularly tested. Licence is GPLv2. The author says the MAC-scan brute force may be added someday, but 'don't hold your breath'.
quotes: Arping is a util to find out if a specific IP address on the LAN is 'taken' and what MAC address owns it.
Sure, you *could* just use 'ping' to find out if it's taken and even if the computer blocks ping (and everything else) you still get an entry in your ARP cache.

Arping tries to drop all possible privileges as early as possible, but this is a network debugging tool, which generates low-level network packets that ordinary users have absolutely no business generating.
